title: The Second Coming of Jesus
subtitle: Both faiths await his return — what each expects him to do reveals everything
summary: Mainstream Islam expects Jesus to return as God's human Messiah, not as God. Detailed teaching comes chiefly from hadith, while Quranic verses about Jesus and the Hour have interpretive differences. His extraordinary return does not itself establish divinity. The Islamic hope is that truth and justice will prevail under God's authority, a hope that calls for repentance now rather than prediction or hostility.

seo.metaTitle: The Second Coming of Jesus in Islam and Christianity
seo.metaDescription: Jesus's return in Islamic prophetic teaching and Christian belief, and what judgment, worship, and preparation mean for ordinary life.
keywords: second coming of Jesus in Islam
Mark 13:32 no one knows the hour

sections.title: An Extraordinary Future Does Not Make the Messiah God
sections.body:
Islam's expectation of Jesus's return is another reason Muslims cannot be indifferent to him. The Messiah remains part of God's plan, returning by God's command rather than sharing God's identity.

This is a claim about revelation and the unseen, not a conclusion that can be read from present events. Readers first testing Islamic sources can begin with [Who Is Prophet Muhammad?](/articles/who-is-prophet-muhammad).

sections.title: What Are We Waiting for—and How Should We Live?
sections.body:
Christianity and Islam both give Jesus an extraordinary future role. They disagree over the identity of the one who returns: the incarnate Son in Christian faith, God's human Messiah in Islam.

That disagreement affects the present. Does love of Jesus mean worshiping him, or sharing his submission to God? Waiting for him cannot replace the responsibility to answer that question or to act justly now.

sections.title: Could Someone With This Role Be Merely Human?
sections.body:
A Christian can ask why Jesus, rather than another prophet, receives such a distinctive end-times role. Islam answers that extraordinary appointment is not divine identity. A Creator able to create and raise a human being can also return that person for a special mission.

That establishes possibility, not proof that the return will happen. Muslim certainty about it rests on accepted revelation. The role must be understood through those sources rather than treated as a standalone argument that Jesus is God.

sections.title: Distinguish the Quran From Its Interpretation
sections.body:
Quran 43:61 connects the passage about Jesus with the Hour, and 4:159 speaks of belief before his death. The identity of the relevant pronouns and the exact implications are discussed in commentary. Mainstream Muslim teaching reads these with hadith about his descent.

It is more accurate to say the Quranic passages are interpreted in support of the return than to suggest the Quran contains the entire later narrative.

sections.title: What the Descent Reports Actually Add
sections.body:
[Sahih al-Bukhari 2476](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2476) describes Jesus descending as a just ruler, breaking the cross, killing swine, and abolishing jizya. [Sahih Muslim 2937a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2937a) describes his encounter with the Dajjal, the great deceiver, in a longer end-times account.

These claims express a real theological disagreement with Christianity, not simply a shared expectation of the same future. Muslims commonly understand them as vindicating Jesus's service to God and correcting beliefs about him. They are not commands for private people to attack Christians, damage crosses, or stage those events themselves.

sections.title: What the New Testament Says
sections.body:
Acts 1:11 promises that Jesus will return as he ascended. Matthew 24:30 describes the Son of Man coming with power and glory. These passages ground the Christian hope that Jesus returns as king and judge.

The same discourse also warns against date-setting. Matthew 24:36 and Mark 13:32 say that no one knows the Hour, and Mark explicitly includes the Son among those who do not know. Christians commonly explain this through Jesus's human nature; Muslims see it as consistent with a prophet whose knowledge is given by God.

The texts therefore establish both expectation and humility: Jesus returns, but human beings do not control the timetable.

sections.title: Shared Expectation Is Not Proof of Either Theology
sections.body:
Christianity's expectation of a divine judge belongs to its wider understanding of Jesus. Islam's expectation belongs to its account of a Messiah who never ceases to be God's servant. A future role cannot decide the question without examining the sources that describe it.

The Islamic account preserves a distinction useful throughout the discussion: God can grant a creature exceptional honor and authority without granting the creature God's right to worship. Jesus's return completes a mission; it does not make the messenger the One who sent him.

sections.title: End-Times Belief Is Not a Political Timetable
sections.body:
Neither frightening headlines nor a self-proclaimed savior gives someone authority to identify a neighbor as an end-times enemy. The reports do not suspend moral duties toward real people living now.

Muslims should also distinguish well-attested reports from popular additions. Uncertain details about sequence, dates, marriage, or burial must not be treated as one indisputable scriptural narrative. Readiness means faith, repentance, and justice, not pretending to control the unseen.

sections.title: Readiness Is a Present Responsibility
sections.body:
Jesus's return is an Islamic affirmation of his extraordinary place among the prophets. It is also a correction: the Messiah returns as God's servant, not as a rival object of worship.

The practical lesson is not speculation about dates. It is readiness—faith in God, repentance, justice, and loyalty to the truth Jesus taught.

sections.title: Be Ready Without Claiming the Date
sections.body:
Islam's invitation is to trust the God who governs the future and to live responsibly in the present. You can honor Jesus's unique mission without making him the Creator, and you can believe in final justice without turning speculation into a way of life.

Read [Jesus as the Messiah](/articles/jesus-as-messiah) to examine the title behind that mission, then [The Day of Judgment](/articles/the-day-of-judgment) for what final accountability asks of every person.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus will return?
A: Yes. The return of Jesus is mainstream doctrine in both Sunni and Shia Islam, grounded in Quran 43:61 and 4:159 as classically interpreted and in numerous narrations in the most authenticated hadith collections.

Q: Does the Quran explicitly describe the second coming?
A: The Quran's references are brief and interpreted in different ways. Mainstream teaching reads 43:61 and 4:159 together with hadith about Jesus's descent; most narrative detail comes from those hadith, not an explicit continuous Quranic account.

Q: Will Jesus bring a new revelation when he returns?
A: No. Mainstream Muslim teaching holds that he returns as a prophet God already sent, ruling by the final revelation rather than bringing a new one, so his return does not conflict with Muhammad being the final prophet.

Q: What do Christians expect Jesus to do at his return?
A: Historic Christian creeds affirm that Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead. Christians differ among themselves over surrounding details such as a rapture or a literal millennium, but the visible return itself is common ground.

Q: Does anyone know when Jesus will return?
A: No. In Mark 13:32 Jesus says that no one knows that day or hour — not the angels, nor the Son, but only the Father — and the Quran places knowledge of the Hour with God alone. Both traditions command readiness, not date-setting.

Q: Why does Jesus not knowing the hour matter for theology?
A: Muslims see limited knowledge as consistent with a human prophet. Christians explain Mark 13:32 through the incarnation, with further differences over how Christ's human knowledge relates to his divinity. The verse is evidence to weigh in that larger discussion, not a refutation that works without addressing their explanation.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **Jesus in the Qur'an** — Geoffrey Parrinder. A respected Christian scholar’s survey of every Quranic passage about Jesus, including the verses on his being raised and his link to the Hour.
- **The Muslim Jesus: Sayings and Stories in Islamic Literature** — Tarif Khalidi. An anthology showing how deeply Muslim civilization revered and remembered Jesus across the centuries.
- **Jesus: Prophet of Islam** — Muhammad 'Ata ur-Rahim and Ahmad Thomson. A Muslim argument for Jesus as prophet rather than incarnate God, engaging Christian history and doctrine.
- **Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium** — Bart D. Ehrman. A secular historian’s reconstruction of Jesus as a preacher of the coming kingdom — useful background on the earliest Christian expectation of the end.
